meaning: “Just as ...”: doing something, or something happening, exactly the way it was said, written, thought, or planned.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + とおりに; noun + の + とおりに; noun + どおりに

senses.label: Do as said / shown
senses.meaning: Doing something exactly the way someone said, did, or wrote it: “just as ...”, “the way ...”. Often used with 「言う」, 「教える」, 「書いてある」, and 「見る」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + とおりに (言ったとおりに・書いてあるとおりに)
examples: Please write it just as the teacher said.
I tried doing it the way the manual says.
Please repeat after me slowly, just as I say it.

senses.label: After nouns
senses.meaning: After a noun, it means following what that noun shows. With 「noun + の + とおり」 it is read 「とおり」; directly after a noun it becomes 「どおり」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + とおりに / noun + どおりに (予定どおり・時間どおり・計画通り)
examples: If you follow the map, you'll get to the station.
The train arrived right on time.
Construction is going according to plan.

senses.label: Just as ...
senses.meaning: 「〜とおりだ／〜とおり、」 means things really are as thought or said. Often used to confirm a prediction or agree with someone. 「そのとおりです」 means “Exactly.”
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / noun + とおり、／とおりだ (思ったとおり・予想どおりだ)
examples: Just as I thought, he didn't come.
The result was just as expected.
You're absolutely right.

notes: Directly after a noun it's read 「どおり」; after 「の」 it's 「とおり」: ✕「予定とおり」→ ○「予定どおり」 or 「予定のとおり」.
The verb's tense decides which words you're following: 「先生が言ったとおりに」 = as the teacher has (already) said; 「私が言うとおりに」 = as I'm (about to) tell you.
To agree with a superior or client, say 「おっしゃるとおりです」. 「あなたの言うとおりです」 sounds rude because of 「あなた」 and the plain form.
「思ったとおり」 means “just as I expected”, while 「思いどおりにならない」 means “things don't go the way you want” — don't mix them up.

daily.title: Learning to cook
daily.description: A family member reminds you to follow the recipe step by step.
daily.example: If you make it just like the recipe says, it won't fail.

daily.title: Giving a friend directions
daily.description: Telling a friend to follow the map you sent.
daily.example: Come the way the map I sent shows, OK?

daily.title: Agreeing with a friend
daily.description: Your friend is spot on, and you fully agree.
daily.example: Yeah, that's exactly right.

work.title: Updating your boss
work.description: Explaining that a project is on schedule.
work.example: The project is proceeding on schedule.

work.title: Training a new hire
work.description: A senior colleague tells a newcomer to follow the manual.
work.example: Please operate it exactly as written in the manual.

etymology: 「とおり」 is written 「通り」, the noun form of the verb 「通る」 (to pass through). It first meant “a road people pass along”, then “the same route or way of doing things”, which gave the meaning “just as ...”. After a noun, the first sound becomes voiced: 「どおり」.
formation: 「〜とおりに」 = the noun 「とおり（通り）」 + the case particle 「に」. 「通り」 is the nominalized masu-stem of the verb 「通る」; its basic meaning is “the road people walk along”, extended to “the way of going, the manner”. The verb or noun before it specifies “which road” (「言ったとおり」 = the road that was described), and adding 「に」 makes it modify the following action: “do it along that road” → “do it the way ...”. Ending with 「だ」 means “matching that road” → “just as ...”. When it attaches directly to a noun, the two form a compound and the first sound of the second element becomes voiced (rendaku), giving 「どおり」.

similar.title: 〜ように (as stated)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning — both can be translated as “as ...”. 「ように」 is mostly used to introduce an explanation (「前に述べたように」); 「とおりに」 stresses doing something exactly the same way, matching the model precisely (「言われたとおりに書く」).

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: 「〜に従って」 also means “in accordance with”, but it's more formal and mostly follows nouns like rules, instructions, or orders (「指示に従って避難する」), emphasizing obedience. 「とおりに」 can attach directly to verbs like 「言った」 or 「書いてある」 and is more conversational.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: 「〜に沿って」 (N2) means “in line with” a policy, plan, or expectation (「方針に沿って進める」) and is fairly formal. 「とおりに」 emphasizes that the result is identical to the model.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from the verbs 「通る／通す」. 「通り」 extended from “the road one passes along” to “the same way”, while 「〜通す」 (「読み通す」) keeps the sense of “going all the way through”, meaning to carry something through to the end.

meaning: 「〜間」 means the main clause continues throughout the whole period; 「〜間に」 means something happens at one point within that period; 「AとBの間」 means “between” in space or among people.
connection: Verb ている form / dictionary form / ない form, い-adjective, な-adjective + な, noun + の + 間(に); noun A と noun B の 間

senses.label: Throughout the period
senses.meaning: 「〜間」 means the state or action in the second clause continues for the whole period. The second clause often uses 「〜ている」 or 「ずっと」. Like “the whole time ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / noun + の + 間、(second clause: continuous action or state)
examples: I was in the countryside the whole summer vacation.
While my mother was cooking, I was cleaning my room.
I read a book the whole time I was on the train.

senses.label: At some point within
senses.meaning: 「〜間に」 means a one-time action or change happens at some point before the period ends. Like “while ...” or “during ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / dictionary form, noun + の + 間に (second clause: one-time action)
examples: A burglar broke in while I was away.
I did the laundry while the kids were asleep.
I want to climb Mt. Fuji while I'm in Japan.

senses.label: Between
senses.meaning: Shows space, time, or relationships between things or people: “between ..., among ...”. 「AとBの間」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun A + と + noun B + の + 間 (に)
examples: There's a bank between the station and the post office.
This app is popular among young people.

notes: With 「間」 the second clause is a state that lasts through the whole period; with 「間に」 it's a one-time event within it. Mixing them up makes the sentence nonsensical: ✕「寝ている間、電話が来た」→ ○「寝ている間に、電話が来た」.
Verbs usually come in the 「ている」 form to show duration: ✕「電車に乗る間、本を読んだ」→ ○「電車に乗っている間、本を読んだ」.
「この間」 usually means “the other day”, not “during this time”: 「この間、田中さんに会った」 = I met Tanaka the other day.
To stress “while ... still holds (before it's too late)”, use 「うちに」: 「熱い間に食べて」 is unnatural →○「熱いうちに食べて」.
「間に合う」 is read 「まにあう」 and means “to make it in time” — it has nothing to do with this pattern: 「電車に間に合った」 = I caught the train.

daily.title: Asking a friend for help
daily.description: Asking a friend to look after your pet while you're away.
daily.example: Could you take care of my cat while I'm on my trip?

daily.title: Doing chores
daily.description: Doing something else while the washing machine runs.
daily.example: I'll go shopping while the washing machine is running.

daily.title: Remembering a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend about your time studying abroad.
daily.example: While I was studying abroad, I kept a diary in Japanese every day.

daily.title: Watching a child grow
daily.description: Being amazed at how fast a child grows.
daily.example: You've grown so much since I last saw you!

work.title: Handing over before a vacation
work.description: Asking a coworker to handle things while you're off.
work.example: While I'm on vacation, Tanaka-san will be in charge of this.

work.title: Meeting preparations
work.description: Explaining what should be done during the meeting.
work.example: Please print out the materials while we're in the meeting.

work.title: Assigning tasks
work.description: A boss asks you to prepare materials during a meeting.
work.example: While the meeting is going on, please make copies of the materials.

etymology: 「間 (あいだ)」 first meant the gap between two things, that is, “between” in space. It was later used for time, meaning the period between two points. Adding 「に」 places an action at one point within that period.
formation: 「〜間（に）」 = the noun 「間（あいだ）」 (the gap between two things) + (the case particle 「に」). Think of time as a line: the preceding action or state marks off a stretch “between two ends”. With 「間」 alone, the second clause covers that whole stretch, so it must be a state or action that lasts from start to finish. Adding 「に」, which marks a point in time, places the second clause at one point inside the stretch, so it's a one-time event. Because you're marking off a stretch, the preceding verb usually takes the continuous 「ている」 form. If this “stretch between two ends” is placed in space or among people, it gives the original meaning, as in 「AとBの間」 and 「若者の間で」.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「うちに」 also means “while ...”, but carries urgency: “while the situation hasn't changed yet, before it's too late” (「若いうちに旅行しよう」). 「間に」 just objectively marks a time span with a clear start and end.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Both can express two things happening at the same time. 「ながら」 requires the same subject doing two actions at once (「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」); with 「間」 the subjects can differ (「母が料理を作っている間、私は掃除した」).

similar.title: 〜中 (じゅう / ちゅう)
similar.explanation: 「〜中（じゅう）」 after a time noun also means “throughout the period” (「夏休み中、ずっと田舎にいた」) and is more concise than 「〜の間」. But it can't follow a verb clause — with verbs you need 「〜間」.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「最中に」 (N3) means “right in the middle of ...”, usually followed by an unexpected interruption (「会議の最中に電話が鳴った」). 「間に」 is just an objective time span, without the “of all times” nuance.

meaning: Marks a deadline: the action must be done by that time. Like “by ...”.
connection: Noun + までに; verb dictionary form + までに

senses.label: Noun deadline
senses.meaning: After a time noun, it shows a deadline. The second clause is a one-time action that gets completed. Like “by ...”.
senses.connection: Time noun + までに (金曜日までに・5時までに・明日までに)
examples: Please hand in your report by Friday.
I'll be back by five.
Please give me an answer by tomorrow.

senses.label: Verb deadline
senses.meaning: After a verb in dictionary form, it means one thing gets done before something else happens. Often used with 「〜ておく」 for getting ready in advance.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までに (〜が来るまでに・〜が終わるまでに)
examples: I want to read this book before summer vacation ends.
Let's tidy up the room before he comes.

senses.label: までには
senses.meaning: Adding 「は」 gives 「までには」, which is softer. It means “at least by then”, and often goes with guesses and wishes.
senses.connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + までには (〜と思う／〜たい)
examples: I think I'll be back by evening.
I want to get married by next spring.

notes: 「まで」 is followed by a continuing action, 「までに」 by a one-time action; mix them up and the meaning changes: ✕「5時までに働く」→ ○「5時まで働く」. 「5時まで待つ」 = wait until 5; 「5時までに来る」 = come by 5.
The verb before it is always in the dictionary form, even when talking about the past: ✕「彼が来たまでに」→ ○「彼が来るまでに、部屋を片付けた」.
In business, setting a deadline with a blunt 「金曜日までに出してください」 sounds like an order. To clients or superiors, 「金曜日までにご提出いただけますと幸いです」 is more appropriate.
「今までに」 and 「これまでに」 mean “so far”, not a deadline: 「今までに三回行った」 = I've been there three times so far.

daily.title: Curfew
daily.description: Parents tell their child what time to be home.
daily.example: Be home by ten.

daily.title: Returning a book
daily.description: A librarian tells someone when a book is due.
daily.example: Please return this book by next Monday.

daily.title: Getting ready for a party
daily.description: Planning with a roommate to be ready before the guests arrive.
daily.example: Let's have the food ready before everyone gets here.

work.title: Giving a task
work.description: A manager tells a staff member the deadline.
work.example: Please put these materials together before tomorrow's meeting.

work.title: Setting a deadline by email
work.description: Asking someone in a business email to reply by a certain date.
work.example: We're sorry to trouble you, but could you reply by the end of this month?

etymology: 「まで」 is generally thought to come from 「真手 (まて)」, a limit you reach. Adding the time particle 「に」 shrinks “up to that limit” into “at some point before the limit”, which gives the deadline meaning.
formation: 「〜までに」 = the adverbial particle 「まで」 (the limit “up to”) + the case particle 「に」 (a point in time). 「まで」 marks an end point, and 「に」 pins the action to a single point; together they mean “(completed) at some point before reaching that limit”. That's why it's followed by a one-time action, not a continuing one; without 「に」, 「まで」 means the action keeps going up to the end point. Since the end point is a limit not yet reached, the verb before it is in the dictionary form.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: Same origin, and the easiest to confuse. 「まで」 means something continues until a time (「3時まで寝た」); 「までに」 means something is completed at some point before that time (「3時までに起きる」), with a sense of a deadline.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Both relate to “before a time”. 「前に」 only states the order of two events (「寝る前に歯を磨く」); 「までに」 draws a deadline that must not be passed (「寝るまでに宿題を終わらせる」).

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「〜ないうちに」 can also be translated “before ...” (「暗くならないうちに帰ろう」), but it stresses “hurry and do it before things change”. 「までに」 uses a clear point in time as the deadline, without that emotional urgency.

meaning: After a dictionary-form verb it sets out a purpose, and the main clause says what is needed or what method is best. After a noun for a person it gives an evaluation or ability from that person's standpoint, “for ..., to ...”; in letters it can also mark a respected person.
connection: Dictionary-form verb / some suru-nouns + には (purpose); noun for a person + には (evaluation, ability, respect)

senses.label: What it takes
senses.meaning: The first clause gives a purpose; the second says what conditions, money, or time it takes. The second clause is often 「必要だ」, 「〜なければならない」, or 「かかる」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には、〜が必要だ／〜なければならない／〜がかかる
examples: To get to the station, you need to take a bus.
To get into this university, you have to pass an exam.
Building a house costs a lot of money.

senses.label: Evaluation / recommendation
senses.meaning: The second clause says which method or place is best. It is often 「〜がいい」, 「〜がいちばんだ」, or 「便利だ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には、〜がいい／〜がいちばんだ／〜に便利だ
examples: The best way to get good at Japanese is to speak it every day.
This park is a good place for taking photos.

senses.label: After nouns
senses.meaning: Some nouns for actions (合格, 上達, 健康, etc.) can take 「には」 directly. This sounds a bit formal.
senses.connection: Suru-noun + には (合格には・上達には・健康には)
examples: Passing takes daily effort.
Improving takes time.

senses.label: For ... (evaluation)
senses.meaning: Evaluates something from a certain person's standpoint. Like “for ...” or “too ... for ...”. Usually followed by evaluative words like 「難しい」, 「大きすぎる」, or 「無理だ」.
senses.connection: Person + には + adjective (難しい, 大きい, 無理だ, etc.)
examples: This problem is hard for children.
These clothes are too big for me.

senses.label: ... can / can't
senses.meaning: Marks who has (or lacks) the ability or perception. Often used with 「できる」, 「分かる」, and 「見える」, with a contrastive feel: “I, for one, can't ...”.
senses.connection: Person + には + できる／分かる／見える, etc.
examples: I could never do something like that.
I can't understand how he feels.

senses.label: Letters: a respected person
senses.meaning: In letters and speeches, 「〜には」 is used instead of 「〜は」 to mark the other person respectfully. It is written and formal.
senses.connection: Respected person + には + お元気で／お変わりなく, etc.
examples: I trust that you are all doing well.

notes: The second clause should say what's needed or what's best — not a specific action the speaker has already decided on: ✕「駅へ行くには、バスに乗ります」→ ○「駅へ行くには、バスに乗るといい」. For your own actions, use 「ために」.
After a person or a noun, it usually means “for (someone), to (someone)” — a completely different meaning: 「子どもには難しい」 = difficult for children, not “in order to (benefit) children”.
「〜にとって」 cannot be used for ability: ✕「私にとってそんなことはできない」→ ○「私にはそんなことはできない」.
Saying 「私にはできません」 or 「私には無理です」 to a superior or client sounds like a flat refusal, or even like dodging responsibility. Soften it: 「私では力不足かもしれませんが…」 or 「少し難しいかと存じます」.
In letters, 「〜には」 (「皆様にはお元気で…」) shows respect toward the reader. It is only used for the other person, never for yourself: ✕「私にはお元気で過ごしております」.

daily.description: A tourist asks a local how to get to a sight.
daily.example: Which bus should I take to get to the temple?

daily.description: A friend wants to lose weight, and you give advice.
daily.example: If you want to lose weight, exercise is the best way.

daily.title: Trying on clothes ordered online
daily.description: Finding that the size doesn't fit.
daily.example: This size might be a little small for me.

work.description: Explaining in a meeting what the project needs to succeed.
work.example: To make this project a success, we need more staff.

work.title: Job requirements
work.description: A job listing states how to apply.
work.example: To apply, you need to submit a résumé.

work.example: This job is too much of a burden for me.

work.title: Writing a greeting letter
work.description: The opening of a seasonal greeting letter from a company to a client.
work.example: We are delighted to hear of your company's continued prosperity.

etymology: The particle 「に」 marks a goal or destination, and 「は」 makes it the topic. 「〜するには」 literally means “as for the goal of doing ...”, which became “if you want to do ...”. The other use of 「〜には」 follows a noun for a person: 「に」 points out “for whom” (the person whose evaluation or ability is in question) and 「は」 makes it the topic with a contrastive tone, giving “for ..., as far as ... is concerned”.
formation: 「〜には」 = verb dictionary form + the case particle 「に」 (goal, destination) + the topic particle 「は」. 「に」 first sets up the action as “the goal to be reached”, then 「は」 brings that goal up as the topic: “as for the goal of doing ...”. So the second clause explains or evaluates that goal — what it takes, how much it costs, what method is best. Because the whole sentence is commenting on a goal rather than narrating an action, the second clause doesn't contain the speaker's own specific volitional act. After a noun for a person, 「に」 marks the person to whom an evaluation, ability or feeling belongs and 「は」 raises that person as the topic with a contrastive sense, “as far as this person goes”, as in 「私には無理だ」. The honorific use in letters borrows the indirectness of 「に」 to avoid addressing the reader directly with 「は」, which sounds more formal. Both uses are 「に」 (point of arrival) + 「は」 (topic); the only difference is whether what precedes is “a goal to be reached” or “the person to whom an evaluation belongs”.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Both express purpose. After 「ために」 comes a specific action taken to reach the goal (「合格するために勉強する」); after 「には」 comes a requirement or evaluation (「合格するには勉強が必要だ」).

similar.title: 〜のに (use / purpose)
similar.explanation: 「のに」 is usually followed by 「使う・便利だ・役に立つ」 to describe a use (「料理するのに使う」); 「には」 is usually followed by 「必要だ・いい・かかる」, with a stronger sense of setting up a goal. The two are often interchangeable in 「〜には／〜のに時間がかかる」.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: Both translate as “for ...”. 「〜にとって」 makes a value judgment from someone's standpoint and is often followed by 「大切だ」 or 「問題だ」. 「〜には」 is more conversational, usually followed by direct evaluations like easy/hard or big/small, and can also express ability (「私にはできない」), which 「〜にとって」 cannot.

similar.title: 〜にしたら・〜にすれば
similar.explanation: Also means “from ...'s standpoint”, but focuses on putting yourself in someone else's shoes and guessing their feelings: 「母にしたら、心配なのだろう」. With 「〜には」, the speaker directly makes an evaluation or judgment.

meaning: Shows what something is made from. Use 「で」 when you can still see the original material, and 「から」 when you can't.
connection: Noun + で／から + 作る (作られる・できている)

senses.label: で: materials
senses.meaning: You can still see the material in the finished product. Like “made of ...”: a table made of wood, a paper plane.
senses.connection: Material noun + で + (〜を) 作る／作られる
examples: I made this desk out of wood.
I made a box out of a milk carton.
This doll is made of paper.

senses.label: から: raw materials
senses.meaning: The raw material has been processed and changed, so you can't see it in the product. Like “made from ...”: wine from grapes, tofu from soybeans.
senses.connection: Raw material noun + から + 作る／作られる
examples: Wine is made from grapes.
Sake is made from rice.
Tofu is made from soybeans.

senses.label: でできている
senses.meaning: 「〜でできている」 and 「〜からできている」 describe what something consists of. They describe a state. The で / から distinction is the same as above.
senses.connection: Noun + で／から + できている／できた
examples: This house is made of stone.
Water is made up of hydrogen and oxygen.

notes: Use 「で」 when the raw material is still recognizable in the product, and 「から」 when it's been chemically transformed: 「ワインはぶどうから作る」 is more natural than 「ぶどうで作る」, while 「木で作った机」 uses 「で」.
Don't map “make A into B” word for word: ✕「牛乳パックを箱に作った」→ ○「牛乳パックで箱を作った」.
The 「で」 in 「台所で作る」「自分で作る」「三人で作る」 marks place, manner, or number of people — not material. Check whether the noun before 「で」 is actually a material of the product.
「〜からできている」 can also mean “consist of”: 「委員会は五人からできている」 — what comes before it doesn't have to be a physical material.

daily.title: Arts and crafts
daily.description: A child shows a parent something they made.
daily.example: I made this out of paper cups.

daily.title: Local specialties
daily.description: A tour guide introduces a local product.
daily.example: These sweets are made from local rice.

daily.title: Talking about furniture
daily.description: A friend compliments your table, and you explain what it's made of.
daily.example: I had this table made out of old wood.

work.title: Introducing a product
work.description: Telling a client what a product is made from.
work.example: This product is made from recycled plastic.

work.title: Explaining materials
work.description: A shop clerk tells a customer what a bag is made of.
work.example: This bag is made of genuine leather.

etymology: 「で」 is the particle for means and materials, from the classical 「にて」. 「から」 originally marks a starting point: the raw material is where the change starts on the way to becoming a product. That is why it's used when the original form can't be seen.
formation: 「で作る」 = noun + the case particle 「で」 (means, what you rely on) + 「作る」; 「から作る」 = noun + the case particle 「から」 (starting point) + 「作る」. 「で」 treats the material as “what you use” to make something, and the material stays as it is in the product, so it's used when the original form is visible. 「から」 treats the raw material as a “point of departure” that changes into something else, so it's used when the original form can't be seen. By the same logic, 「〜でできている」 and 「〜からできている」 are chosen according to whether the material keeps its original form.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: Same origin: material 「で」 is a kind of means 「で」. A means is an external tool (「はしで食べる」), while a material becomes part of the product (「木で作る」). Check whether the thing remains in the finished product.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the basic meaning of 「から」 is a starting point in time or space (「駅から歩く」). For raw materials it's “the starting point of a change” — the material is processed into something else, so it's mostly used when the original form can't be seen.

meaning: “In case ...”, “If ...”: imagines a situation and says what to do if it happens. Common in rules, notices, and instructions.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form / nai-form, i-adjective, na-adjective + な, noun + の + 場合 (は)

senses.label: Hypothetical case
senses.meaning: Imagines a situation, and the second clause gives what to do or the rule. Common in notices, manuals, and rules. More formal than 「〜たら」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form / nai-form, noun + の + 場合は (雨の場合は・遅れる場合は)
examples: In case of rain, the game will be canceled.
If you're going to be late, be sure to let us know.
In case of fire, do not use the elevators.

senses.label: As for someone
senses.meaning: 「Noun + の場合 (は)」 can also mean “in the case of ...”, picking out a specific person or thing.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 場合 (は)、〜 (私の場合は・子どもの場合)
examples: In my case, I commute by train every morning.
For children, the fee is half price.

notes: 「場合」 is used for hypotheticals or general rules, not for narrating a specific one-time event that actually happened: ✕「昨日財布をなくした場合、交番に行きました」→ ○「なくしたとき、交番に行きました」.
The tense before it changes the meaning: 「遅れる場合は連絡してください」 = contact us (in advance) if you expect to be late; 「遅れた場合は」 = in case you've already been late.
「場合」 is read 「ばあい」, not 「ばごう」 — both kanji use their native Japanese (kun) readings.
「場合によっては」 means “depending on the situation, possibly even”, and 「〜場合が多い」 means “in many cases” — neither is a hypothetical condition.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Agreeing in advance what to do if it rains.
daily.example: If it rains, shall we go to a movie?

daily.title: Station announcement
daily.description: A sign at a station informs passengers.
daily.example: If you have left something behind, please tell a station attendant.

work.title: Leave rules
work.description: Company rules explain how to take a day off.
work.example: If you will be absent, contact your manager before work starts.

work.title: Contract terms
work.description: A contract states what happens if a term is broken.
work.example: If payment is not made by the deadline, the contract will be terminated.

work.title: Customer service
work.description: A customer service rep explains the return policy.
work.example: If there is a defect in the product, we will exchange it.

etymology: 「場合」 is made of 「場」 (place) and 「合い」 (meeting). It first meant “the place where a situation comes up”, that is, “occasion, case”. With 「は」 as the topic marker, it introduces a hypothetical case.
formation: 「場合」 = 「場（ば: place）」 + 「合い（あい: meeting, coming together）」; its basic meaning is “the scene where things come together”, i.e. “a situation, a case”. The preceding clause specifies “which situation”, and the topic particle 「は」 sets it up as the topic: “in the case of ... (here's what to do)”. Because it sets up a situation as a “scene” rather than narrating something that happened, it's naturally suited to hypotheticals, rules, and explaining countermeasures.

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 「とき」 can refer to a moment that actually happened (「昨日帰ったとき」); 「場合」 is only for hypotheticals or general rules, sounds more formal, and is common in notices, regulations, and manuals.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is conversational and widely used; 「場合は」 is more formal and often sets up “a situation that might arise” before explaining what to do (「火事の場合は、エレベーターを使わないでください」).

similar.title: 〜際（に）
similar.explanation: 「際（に）」 (N3) is a formal version of 「とき」, usually referring to the actual time you do something (「ご利用の際は」). 「場合」 focuses on “if this situation should arise” and is more hypothetical.

meaning: “You just need to ...”, “All you have to do is ...”: gives advice or a method. As a question, it asks “What should I do?” It can also express a wish.
connection: Verb / adjective ba-form + いい (書けばいい・安ければいい)

senses.label: Advice / method
senses.meaning: Tells someone how to reach their goal: “just do this and it's fine”. It sounds relaxed, sometimes with a hint of “it's easy”.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + いい (〜ばいいです／〜ばいいよ)
examples: If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.
You just need to take this medicine three times a day.
You can just take the bus to the station.

senses.label: Asking what to do
senses.meaning: With a question word, it asks what you should do: “What should I ...?” Common when asking for advice or help.
senses.connection: Question word + verb ba-form + いいですか／いいでしょうか
examples: What should I do?
What should I bring?

senses.label: Wish
senses.meaning: 「〜ばいいなあ」 hopes something will come true. 「〜ばいいのに」 shows dissatisfaction with how things are and wishes they were different, with a sense of regret.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ba-form + いいなあ／いいのに
examples: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
I wish I lived closer to the station.

notes: Saying 「〜ばいいじゃない」 or 「〜ばいいでしょ」 to someone sounds impatient and cold — “well, just do ..., then”: 「自分でやればいいじゃない」. Getting this answer when asking for help will annoy the asker.
「〜ばいいのに」 aimed at someone else is a reproach — “you could have just ... (why didn't you?)”: 「言えばいいのに」. Don't use it to superiors or clients.
The ba-form conjugation is the most common mistake: ✕「行くばいい」→ ○「行けばいい」; ✕「安いばいい」→ ○「安ければいい」; する becomes 「すれば」: ✕「どうしればいい」→ ○「どうすればいい」.
When suggesting something to a superior, avoid 「〜ばいいですよ」 and use 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 instead.

daily.title: Giving a friend an idea
daily.description: A friend doesn't know how to contact a teacher, so you make a suggestion.
daily.example: Why don't you just send an email?

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Asking station staff where to change trains.
daily.example: Where should I change trains to get to Shinjuku?

daily.title: Looking forward to the weekend
daily.description: Talking with family about a weekend outing.
daily.example: I hope the weather's nice on Sunday.

work.title: Asking a senior colleague
work.description: A new employee checks how to do a task.
work.example: Who should I submit these documents to?

work.title: Explaining how to submit
work.description: Telling a client that submitting documents is easy.
work.example: You can just send us the documents by email.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「ば」 and the adjective 「いい (良い)」: literally “it's good if ...”. From “it's fine once the condition is met” came the uses for advice, asking what to do, and wishes.
formation: 「〜ばいい」 = the hypothetical 「ば」 + the adjective 「いい（良い）」, literally “if ..., (it's) good”. The speaker simply puts forward one condition and says meeting it is “good”, so it becomes advice: “all you need to do is ...”. As a question, 「どうすればいい？」 asks “what condition should be met for it to be good?”. When the condition hasn't come true and is out of one's control (「晴れれば」), “if ..., it'd be good” becomes a wish. Precisely because it only stresses “meeting the condition is enough”, using it in reply to someone can sound like “what's so hard about that?”.

similar.title: 〜たらいい
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning; both 「どうすればいい」 and 「どうしたらいい」 are very common for asking how to do something. 「ばいい」 stresses “meeting this condition is enough”, while 「たらいい」 is more conversational.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is clear advice after a comparison, fairly strong, sometimes a warning (「行ったほうがいい」). 「ばいい」 just points out one workable method — “doing this will do”.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: Same origin: changing 「いい」 to its past form 「よかった」 turns “doing this would be good” into “it would have been good if I'd done this”, expressing regret about the past.

meaning: Means “it would be good if…”: said to another person it is gentle advice; in question form it asks “what should I do”; about things outside one's control it expresses a wish or good wishes, “I hope that…”.
connection: Verb / adjective た-form + らいい (行ったらいい); verb / adjective plain present + といい (晴れるといいね); + な・ね・のに・けど

senses.label: Advice
senses.meaning: Suggests that doing something would be a good idea. It sounds gentle, softer than 「〜ほうがいい」. Often 「〜たらいいよ」 or 「〜たらいいと思う」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らいい (よ)／らいいと思う
examples: If you're tired, you should take a little rest.
I think you should talk to the teacher about it.

senses.label: Asking what to do
senses.meaning: With a question word, it asks what you should do. One of the most common ways to ask for help in daily life.
senses.connection: Question word + verb ta-form + らいいですか／らいいでしょうか
examples: What should I do?
Where should I submit this document?

senses.label: Hope
senses.meaning: 「〜たらいいなあ」 hopes something will happen. 「〜たらいいのに」 wishes for something contrary to reality, with a sense of regret.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective ta-form + らいいなあ／らいいのに
examples: I hope the weather's good tomorrow.
It would be nice to live in Japan someday.
I can't wait for summer vacation. I hope I can go to the beach.

senses.label: Wishing someone well
senses.meaning: Expresses a kind hope about someone else's situation: “I hope ...”. Usually 「〜といいですね」 or 「〜といいね」. The tone is gentle and warm.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form・nai-form + といいですね／といいね
examples: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
I hope you pass the exam.

senses.label: Unmet wish / worry
senses.meaning: 「〜といいのに／たらいいのに」 expresses regret that reality differs from your wish. 「〜といいんだけど」 means “I hope so, but I'm a little worried”.
senses.connection: Plain form + といいのに／といいんだけど; verb ta-form + らいいのに
examples: I wish the holidays were longer.
I hope he makes it in time, but I'm not sure.
I wish every day were Sunday.

notes: 「〜たらいいですか」 asks “what should I do?”, while 「〜てもいいですか」 asks for permission — different meanings: 「ここに座ったらいいですか」 = Should I sit here?; 「ここに座ってもいいですか」 = May I sit here?
Saying 「〜たらいいですよ」 to superiors or elders sounds like you're instructing them; use 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 instead.

The sentence-final particle decides the meaning: 「早く寝るといいよ」 is advice (“you should go to bed early”), while 「早く寝られるといいね」 is a wish (“I hope you can get to bed early”). Change 「ね」 to 「よ」 and a good wish turns into instruction.
For something that has already happened but whose result is unknown, use 「〜ているといい」: ✕「無事に着いたといいね」→ ○「無事に着いているといいね」.
The sound changes of the ta-form are easy to get wrong: ✕「休みたらいい」→ ○「休んだらいい」; ✕「書きたらいい」→ ○「書いたらいい」.

daily.title: A friend can't sleep
daily.description: A friend says they can't sleep, and you give advice.
daily.example: You should try not to look at your phone before bed.

daily.title: Lost and asking for help
daily.description: Asking a passerby for help in an unfamiliar place.
daily.example: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

daily.title: Cheering on a friend
daily.description: A friend is heading to a job interview, and you wish them luck as you part.
daily.example: I hope the interview goes well.

daily.title: Visiting someone in the hospital
daily.description: What you say when visiting a sick friend.
daily.example: I hope you get well soon.

work.title: Asking your boss
work.description: Checking with your boss when you're not sure how to proceed.
work.example: How would you like me to proceed with this matter?

work.title: Advising a coworker
work.description: A coworker has a problem, and you casually suggest something.
work.example: I think you should ask Yamada-san in accounting.

work.title: Mid-project
work.description: Talking with a colleague about a project's progress and sharing your hopes.
work.example: I hope this project finishes on schedule, but...

etymology: Built from the conditional 「たら」 or 「と」 plus the adjective 「いい（良い）」, literally “it would be good if…”. 「たら」 comes from the hypothetical form of the perfective 「た」, and 「と」 is a conditional particle; the sentence stops at the evaluation 「いい」, which gives rise to the advice, question and wish uses.
formation: It combines the conditional 「たら」 (or 「と」) with 「いい（良い）」, literally “it would be good if…”. 「たら」 pictures an action as already done and then evaluates it as “that would be good”. Said to another person it is gentle advice (「休んだらいいよ」); turned into a question it asks “what should I do” (「どうしたらいいですか」); said about something outside one's control it is a wish, “I hope that…” (「晴れるといいね」, 「〜たらいいな」), and 「ね」, 「な」, 「のに」 or 「けど」 can add good wishes, musing, regret or worry. Because the sentence gives only the condition and the evaluation “good”, whether it is advice or a wish depends on the person addressed and the sentence-final particle.

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「ばいい」 stresses “meeting the condition is enough” and is slightly more formal; 「たらいい」 is more conversational and more common when asking for advice (「どうしたらいいですか」).

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: 「たらどうですか」 directly urges the listener to do something in question form and is more assertive; 「たらいい」 states “doing this will be good”, or asks what you yourself should do.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: 「〜てほしい」 says directly “I want someone to do ...”, so the desire is clear, and toward a superior it feels imposing. 「〜といいね」 only says “it'd be nice if ...”, without specifying who does it, so the tone is softer.

similar.title: 〜ないかな (wish)
similar.explanation: 「〜ないかな」 is a wish said to oneself, with a feeling of eager waiting (「早く夏休みにならないかな」); 「〜といいな」 is calmer, just voicing “it'd be nice if ...”. The two are often used together.

similar.title: 〜ば〜のに
similar.explanation: Both 「〜ばいいのに」 and 「〜といいのに」 express regret, “it would be nice if ... (but it isn't)”. When about another person's behavior, 「〜ばいいのに」 often carries blame, “why don't you ...?”.

meaning: Makes a suggestion to the listener: “Why don't you ...?”, “How about ...?”
connection: Verb ta-form + らどうですか (らどう？・らいかがですか)

senses.label: General suggestion
senses.meaning: Actively encourages the listener to do something: “Why don't you ...?” In speech, it's often shortened to 「〜たらどう？」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らどうですか／らどう？ (〜てみたらどう)
examples: Why don't you take a little break?
Why don't you go see a doctor?
Why don't you try asking him directly?

senses.label: Polite suggestion
senses.meaning: 「〜たらいかがですか」 replaces 「どう」 with the more polite 「いかが」. Used with guests, older people, or in customer service.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らいかがですか／らいかがでしょうか
examples: Why don't you take this seat?
Why not give it a try?

senses.label: Annoyance / criticism
senses.meaning: 「〜たらどうなの」 and 「〜たらどうだ」 sound annoyed or pushy: “Why don't you just ...!” Only used with people close to you or people below you.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + らどうなの／らどうだ
examples: Stop complaining and do it yourself, why don't you.
You could at least help a little.

notes: Using 「〜たらどうですか」 to superiors, elders, or clients sounds condescending, as if you're instructing them. In formal situations, say 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」.
「〜たらどう？」「〜たらどうなの」「〜たらどうだ」 with strong intonation are reproaches and show impatience: 「少しは手伝ったらどう？」 = Can't you help out a little?
It's only for suggesting the listener do something on their own. To invite someone to do something with you, use 「〜ませんか」: ✕「一緒に映画を見たらどうですか」→ ○「一緒に映画を見ませんか」.
「〜たらどうなる？」 asks about a result, and 「〜たらどうしよう」 expresses worry — “what if ...?” Neither is a suggestion.

daily.title: A friend has a cold
daily.description: Your friend keeps coughing, and you urge them to see a doctor.
daily.example: Why don't you hurry up and go to the hospital?

daily.title: A friend can't decide on a gift
daily.description: Your friend doesn't know what to give, so you suggest something.
daily.example: Why don't you give her flowers? I'm sure she'll love them.

daily.title: A parent nagging
daily.description: A mother is annoyed with her child who won't get up.
daily.example: It's already ten. Get up already, will you?

work.title: Making a proposal in a meeting
work.description: Suggesting an improvement to colleagues in a meeting.
work.example: How about making the materials a bit simpler?

work.title: Hosting a client
work.description: Politely suggesting a guest take a rest.
work.example: You must be tired after your long trip. Why don't you rest for a while?

etymology: Made of the conditional 「たら」 and 「どうですか」, which asks for an opinion: literally “How would it be if you did ...?” By asking the listener's opinion, it makes a suggestion indirectly.
formation: 「〜たらどうですか」 = the conditional 「たら」 + the question word 「どう」 (how) + 「ですか」. Literally “if you did ..., how would it be?” — it puts an action into a hypothetical and asks the listener to judge the result themselves, making a suggestion indirectly in the form of a question. Because on the surface it leaves the decision to the listener, it's softer than a direct order; but when the speaker clearly thinks “of course you should”, the same question becomes a reproach: “why don't you?”. Using 「いかが」 instead of 「どう」 makes it more polite.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: 「ほうがいい」 is clear advice after a comparison, strong and sometimes a warning (「医者に行ったほうがいい」). 「たらどうですか」 just offers one option and leaves the decision to the listener.

similar.title: 〜たらいい
similar.explanation: 「たらいい」 states “doing this will be good”; 「たらどうですか」 directly urges the listener in question form, which is more assertive and more easily sounds impatient.

similar.title: 〜はどうですか・〜はいかがですか
similar.explanation: Same origin: both ask for an opinion with 「どう／いかが」. 「Noun + はどうですか」 recommends something or asks for an impression (「コーヒーはいかがですか」); 「たらどうですか」 suggests taking an action.

meaning: Expresses regret: “I should have ...”, “I wish I had ...”. What's described didn't actually happen, or the opposite did.
connection: Verb ba-form + よかった (negative: 〜なければよかった)

senses.label: Regret for not doing
senses.meaning: The speaker regrets not doing something. Reality is the opposite of what's said. Like “I should have ...”. Often ends with 「〜なあ」.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + よかった (なあ)
examples: I should have studied more.
I should have brought an umbrella.

senses.label: Regret for doing
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜なければよかった」 regrets doing something: “I shouldn't have ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なければよかった
examples: I shouldn't have said that.
I shouldn't have eaten so much.

senses.label: Regret about others
senses.meaning: 「〜ばよかったのに」, said about someone else, shows pity or mild criticism: “You should have ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + よかったのに
examples: You should have told me sooner.
You should have come too.

notes: Mix up affirmative and negative and you regret the opposite thing: 「言えばよかった」 = I regret not saying it; 「言わなければよかった」 = I regret saying it.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てよかった」: 「来てよかった」 = I'm glad I came (relief); 「来ればよかった」 = I wish I had come (you didn't — regret).
「〜ばよかったのに」 aimed at others is a reproach: 「早く言ってくれればよかったのに」. Saying this to a superior or client is very rude — reflect on yourself instead: 「私から確認すればよかったです」.
Nouns and na-adjectives can't take 「ば」 directly: ✕「学生ばよかった」→ ○「学生ならよかった」「学生だったらよかった」.

daily.title: After an exam
daily.description: Complaining to a friend after doing badly on a test.
daily.example: I should have gone to bed earlier last night.

daily.title: Shopping regret
daily.description: Finding out after buying something that it was cheaper elsewhere.
daily.example: I should have bought it at that other store.

daily.title: A friend missed a party
daily.description: Telling a friend who didn't come that the party was fun.
daily.example: It was fun. You should have come too.

work.title: Reflecting on a mistake
work.description: Reflecting in a meeting after a project ran into trouble.
work.example: I regret that I didn't check more carefully beforehand.

work.title: Warning a staff member
work.description: A manager speaks to someone who didn't report a problem in time.
work.example: If there was a problem, you should have reported it right away.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「ば」 and 「よかった」, the past of 「よい (良い)」: literally “it would have been good if ...”. Because the condition is contrary to fact, it became a set phrase for regret.
formation: 「〜ばよかった」 = the hypothetical 「ば」 + 「よかった」, the past form of 「よい（良い）」; literally “if ..., it would have been good”. The condition is placed in the past and is contrary to fact (you didn't do it, or you did), so the sentence expresses regret: “the choice back then was wrong”. To regret not doing something, use the affirmative 「〜ば」; to regret doing it, use the negative 「〜なければ」. Aimed at someone else, “it would have been good if you had ...” naturally becomes a reproach.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: Both can express regret. 「〜てしまった」 means “I've already done something I shouldn't have” (「言ってしまった」); 「〜ばよかった」 means “I wish I had done that”, regretting the choice made back then.

similar.title: 〜ば〜のに
similar.explanation: 「〜ば〜のに」 is broader: a hypothetical contrary to reality, with regret or dissatisfaction (「お金があれば買えるのに」), and can also refer to the present. 「ばよかった」 is specifically for past regret and is the most common set phrase of this type.

similar.title: 〜ばいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ばいい」 is about the present or future, offering a method or a wish. Changing 「いい」 to its past form 「よかった」 turns it into regret about something past that can't be changed.

meaning: Gives permission or makes a concession: “It's OK to ...”, “I don't mind if ...”. Slightly more formal than 「〜てもいい」.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / na-adjective or noun + で + もかまわない (構わない)

senses.label: Permission
senses.meaning: Allows someone to do something, or asks if it's OK to do it. The question 「〜てもかまいませんか」 is a polite way to ask for permission.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もかまわない／もかまいません (か)
examples: Is it all right to take photos here?
You may use this pen.
If you're tired, it's fine to go home first.

senses.label: Concession / don't mind
senses.meaning: After an adjective or noun, it means “I don't mind if it's ...”, stating a condition you can accept.
senses.connection: i-adjective くて / noun, na-adjective + で + もかまわない
examples: I don't mind if the room is small.
Tomorrow is fine for getting in touch.
I don't mind if it's a bit expensive.

senses.label: Don't have to
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜なくてもかまわない」 means it's fine not to do something: “You don't have to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくてもかまわない
examples: You don't have to come tomorrow.
You don't have to eat all of it.

notes: Asking permission with 「〜てもかまいませんか」 is polite. But volunteering 「〜てもかまいませんよ」 to a superior or client amounts to “granting” them permission and sounds condescending — say 「どうぞ〜てください」 instead.
When answering 「〜てもかまいませんか」, you can't refuse with 「かまいます」; use a soft refusal such as 「すみません、ちょっと…」.
「かまわないで」 on its own means “leave me alone, don't bother about me”: 「私にかまわないで」 — it has nothing to do with permission.
Nouns and na-adjectives take 「でも」: ✕「明日もかまいません」→ ○「明日でもかまいません」.

daily.title: At a friend's house
daily.description: Asking if you can use something at a friend's place.
daily.example: Mind if I use your bathroom?

daily.title: Looking for an apartment
daily.description: Telling a real estate agent what you're looking for.
daily.example: I don't mind if it's a bit far from the station.

daily.title: Meeting up
daily.description: A friend says they'll be late, and you say it's fine.
daily.example: It's fine if you're a little late.

work.title: Checking how to submit
work.description: Checking whether you can send something electronically.
work.example: Would it be all right to send the documents by email?

work.title: Job interview
work.description: A candidate says what conditions they can accept.
work.example: I don't mind being posted outside the city.

etymology: 「かまう (構う)」 means “to mind, to care about”. Its negative 「かまわない」 means “not to mind”. 「〜てもかまわない」 literally means “even if ..., I don't mind”, which gives permission and concession.
formation: 「〜てもかまわない」 = the concessive 「ても」 (even if ...) + 「かまわない」, the negative of the verb 「かまう（構う: to mind, to care about）」. Literally “even if ..., (I) don't mind”. By saying they don't mind it happening, the speaker is effectively allowing the listener to do it, so it becomes permission; after adjectives or nouns (「狭くても」「明日でも」) it's the concession “even if ..., it doesn't matter”. Because the core is “I don't mind”, it carries the speaker's stance and sounds slightly more formal than 「てもいい」.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「てもいい」 is more common and conversational; 「てもかまわない」 is slightly more formal, stresses “I don't mind”, and is often used to ask for or grant permission politely.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Both 「なくてもいい」 and 「なくてもかまわない」 mean “you don't have to ...”; the latter is slightly more formal. Don't confuse them with the prohibition 「〜てはいけない」.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「構う」 (to mind, to care about). 「〜もかまわず」 (N2) means “without regard for ...” (「人目もかまわず泣いた」), describing someone not caring about something they should, often critically.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the first half of this pattern is the concessive 「ても」 (even if). 「ても」 alone only means “even if ...”; followed by 「かまわない」 it becomes a permission expression: “even if ..., I don't mind”.

meaning: Spoken contractions of 「〜なくては」 and 「〜なければ」, mostly meaning “must...” (the following 「いけない」 is often dropped), and also “if one doesn't... (it won't work)”.
connection: Verb ない-form (drop 「い」) + なくちゃ / なきゃ (+ いけない / だめ); + a negative result (conditional)

senses.label: Have to (shortened)
senses.meaning: Drops the 「いけない」 and ends the sentence with 「なくちゃ」 or 「なきゃ」. Usually said to yourself or to people close to you, about something you have to do.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくちゃ／なきゃ。
examples: Oh, look at the time. I've got to go home.
I have to write my report by tomorrow.
I need to go to bed early.

senses.label: Full form
senses.meaning: Followed by 「いけない」 or 「だめ」, it expresses obligation or advice to others. More casual than 「〜なければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なくちゃいけない／なきゃだめ
examples: I have to take my medicine.
You've got to practice every day.

senses.label: Unless ..., not
senses.meaning: As a condition, it means “if you don't do A, B won't happen”. The second clause is usually negative.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + なきゃ／なくちゃ + negative result
examples: If we don't hurry, we won't make it.
You can't tell until you actually see it.

notes: This is casual speech. Saying 「〜なきゃ」 to superiors or clients, or using it in formal writing, sounds too casual; in formal situations use 「〜なければなりません」 or 「〜なくてはいけません」.
Don't confuse it with the prohibitive 「〜ちゃ」 — the meaning is the exact opposite: 「食べなくちゃ」 = I have to eat; 「食べちゃだめ」 = you mustn't eat.
It's formed from the nai-form minus 「い」: ✕「行かないちゃ」→ ○「行かなくちゃ」; ✕「行かないきゃ」→ ○「行かなきゃ」.

A bare 「〜なきゃ」 at the end of a sentence means “must”; when followed by a consequence it is a condition, “if not ...”: 「急がなきゃ、遅刻するよ」 = if you don't hurry, you'll be late. Check whether another clause follows.

daily.title: Before leaving in the morning
daily.description: Muttering to yourself when you see how late it is.
daily.example: Oh no, I have to leave now.

daily.title: Reminding a friend
daily.description: Your friend has a test tomorrow but is still playing.
daily.example: You've got a test tomorrow, right? You need to study.

daily.title: Weekend plans
daily.description: Telling your family what you need to do this weekend.
daily.example: I've got to clean my room this weekend.

daily.title: Getting up in the morning
daily.description: The alarm goes off, and you tell yourself to get up.
daily.example: Oh no, it's already seven. I've gotta get up.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker you're close to what you still need to do.
work.example: I still have to make the materials for this afternoon's meeting.

work.title: Before leaving work
work.description: Telling a coworker you can't leave yet.
work.example: I just need to answer this email. You can go ahead.

etymology: 「なくちゃ」 comes from 「なくては」 by sound change (「ては」→「ちゃ」). 「なきゃ」 comes from 「なければ」 (「ければ」→「けりゃ」→「きゃ」). Both are contractions that arose in speech for speed, and the following 「いけない」 / 「ならない」 is often dropped.
formation: 「〜なくちゃ」 comes from 「〜なくては（いけない）」: the continuative 「なく」 of the negative 「ない」 + 「ては」, with 「ては」 turning into 「ちゃ」 in speech. 「〜なきゃ」 comes from 「〜なければ（ならない）」: 「なければ」→「なけりゃ」→「なきゃ」. Both were originally the condition “if one doesn't...”, followed by an evaluation 「いけない／ならない」 (it's no good): “it's no good not to do...”, a double negative that yields “must...”. In speech the evaluation is easy for the listener to supply and is often dropped, leaving only the condition, so a sentence-final 「なきゃ」 / 「なくちゃ」 itself means “have to...” (the elliptical and full-form senses). If what follows is not 「いけない」 but a concrete negative result, the original conditional meaning is kept: “if one doesn't..., (it won't work)”.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: The full form, more formal and usable in writing and polite situations. 「なきゃ」 is the casual contraction of 「なければ」, and 「なくちゃ」 of 「なくては」; the meaning is the same.

similar.title: 〜ないといけない
similar.explanation: Also very common in speech, with a similar meaning; it too can drop its second half and end with 「〜ないと」 (「もう行かないと」).

similar.title: 〜ないと (if not ...)
similar.explanation: 「〜ないと」 literally means “if (you) don't ... (something bad will happen)” (「急がないと遅れるよ」), and with the second half dropped it also means “must”. 「なきゃ／なくちゃ」 express obligation more directly.

meaning: Something doesn't always happen, but happens now and then: “sometimes ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form, i-adjective + ことがある

senses.label: Sometimes do
senses.meaning: Says someone sometimes does something, or something sometimes happens, but not often. Often used with 「ときどき」 or 「たまに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことがある／ことがあります
examples: I sometimes walk to work.
This train is sometimes late in the morning.
Once in a while I go to the movies alone.

senses.label: Sometimes don't
senses.meaning: After the nai-form, it means “sometimes doesn't ...”: usually it happens, but there are exceptions.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ことがある
examples: When I'm busy, I sometimes skip lunch.
He sometimes doesn't reply to emails.

senses.label: Adjectives
senses.meaning: After an i-adjective, it means a state sometimes occurs. Often used for weather, health, and so on.
senses.connection: i-adjective + ことがある
examples: Around here, it can be cool even in summer.
In spring, it sometimes turns cold suddenly.

notes: The verb form before it decides the meaning: 「日本へ行くことがある」 = I sometimes go to Japan; 「日本へ行ったことがある」 = I've been to Japan (experience).
It only means “occasionally” and can't describe daily habits: ✕「毎朝コーヒーを飲むことがある」→ ○「毎朝コーヒーを飲む」.
In 「話したいことがある」 and 「やることがある」 (“there's something I want to say / something I have to do”), 「こと」 is a real noun and doesn't express frequency.

daily.title: Talking about your habits
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your eating habits.
daily.example: On my days off, I sometimes skip breakfast.

daily.title: Warning a tourist
daily.description: A local warns a tourist about the weather.
daily.example: The weather in the mountains can change suddenly.

work.title: Explaining a system
work.description: Telling a customer what can happen with the system.
work.example: When there's heavy traffic, it can sometimes be hard to connect.

work.title: Explaining work conditions
work.description: In an interview, explaining that overtime or weekend work may come up.
work.example: During busy periods, you may sometimes need to work on Saturdays.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 means “matter, situation”, and 「ある」 means “exist”. 「〜ることがある」 literally means “there exist situations where ...”, so it came to mean “sometimes happens”. With the ta-form, it means “there exists such an experience”, the experience use.
formation: 「〜ることがある」 = verb dictionary form + the formal noun 「こと」 (matter, situation) + 「が」 + 「ある」 (exist). 「こと」 turns the action into a “situation”, and 「がある」 says that situation “exists” — literally “there exists such a thing as ...”. Saying a situation “exists” implies it isn't always the case, only that it does occur, so the meaning is “sometimes ...”. With the dictionary form, which describes general cases, it means something sometimes happens; switch to the ta-form and it means “such a thing has existed”, i.e. experience.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: Same origin and exactly the same structure — only the verb form before it differs. With the ta-form it expresses past experience (「日本へ行ったことがある」); with the dictionary form it means something happens sometimes (「日本へ行くことがある」).

similar.title: めったに〜ない
similar.explanation: Both are about frequency. 「めったに〜ない」 means “hardly ever ...”, an even lower frequency than 「ことがある」, and is negative (「めったに映画を見ない」); 「ことがある」 says affirmatively “occasionally ...”.

similar.title: 〜ことにしている
similar.explanation: Same origin: it also nominalizes an action with 「こと」. 「ことにしている」 expresses a habit you decided on and keep up (「毎朝走ることにしている」); 「ことがある」 just says something happens occasionally, with no sense of deliberately sticking to it.
